source.filename: 2026-A novel frictional contact correction transfer matrix method for bolted vibration systems.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Timoshenko beam theory assuming plane sections remain plane while accounting for shear deformation and rotary inertia
Small angular displacement and small rotation approximations (sin theta approx theta, cos theta approx 1)
Linear elastic isotropic material behavior for metallic components (65Mn spring steel and structural steel)
Linear piezoelectric constitutive relations incorporating complex material moduli to account for mechanical, dielectric, and piezoelectric damping losses
Static frictional contact at bolted interfaces where shear force is much smaller than normal force, representing interface compliance via an equivalent angular correction coefficient
Neglect of local tangential micro-slip and partial slip in the interfacial state vector transfer equations
Rectangular beam cross-section with shear correction factor kappa^2 = 5/6 (0.87 for Timoshenko beam formulation)
control_variables: Bolt tightening torque of 1.6 N*m applied to M4 bolts (calibrated to approximately 823 N preload)
Excitation voltage amplitudes: 50 Vpp (or 50 V) for ZS and NS-2 systems, 10 Vpp for NS-1 system
Nominal geometric dimensions and material properties of structural blocks, connecting plates, PZT plates, bolts, and gaskets
Fixed base constraint boundary conditions for the structural supports
Iterative convergence tolerances (0.001 for ZS, 1 for NS-1 and NS-2 in FCCTMM; 3% for finite element mesh sensitivity)
Friction testing parameters: normal preload of 3 N, offset radius of 6 mm, and test duration of 10 s
dependent_variables: Resonant frequencies of the first and second vibration modes
Vibration mode shapes of the connecting plate
Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) values evaluating mode shape consistency
Computation execution time and computational speedup ratio
Frictional contact correction coefficient (cfc) converged values and iteration numbers
Relative prediction error of resonant frequencies compared to experimental measurements
First-slip interfacial friction coefficient between 65Mn components
Bolt preload generated by applied tightening torque

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Iteratively incorporating a frictional contact correction coefficient into the transfer matrix method accounts for interfacial compliance and separation, substantially improving resonant frequency predictions over rigid-joint transfer matrix models.

Formulating the generalized transfer matrix for elastic beam elements with arbitrary input and output locations enables accurate modeling of asymmetrical and modular structural connections, enhancing mode shape accuracy.

Experimental modal testing using 3D scanning laser Doppler vibrometry confirms that the frictional contact correction transfer matrix method attains first-mode predictive precision comparable to contact finite element analysis while speeding up computation by over 100 times.

Prediction error of the frictional contact correction method increases significantly for the second bending mode due to overcorrection resulting from assuming first-mode shear force distributions across components vibrating in disparate modes.
Tribometer first-slip testing and torque-preload calibration quantify the friction coefficient (0.204) and linear torque-preload relationship governing the contact interface.

experimental_setup: PSV-500-3D Doppler 3D scanning laser vibrometer (Polytec, Germany) with three laser heads, control box, and display
Power amplifier, signal generator, and oscilloscope for piezoelectric excitation and signal acquisition
MFT-5000 multifunctional friction and wear testing machine (Rtec, USA) with rotary table and 3D-printed fixture
Digital torque wrench and ring-type pressure sensor for bolt torque-preload calibration

Three physical bolted prototype assemblies: centrally symmetric Z-type system (ZS), mirror-symmetric N-type system with one PZT pair (NS-1), and mirror-symmetric N-type system with two PZT pairs (NS-2) made of 65Mn, PZT-5J, and structural steel fasteners
future_work: Extending the transfer matrix framework to incorporate tangential micro-slip effects and detailed contact mechanics (friction coefficient and preload dependence) for lap-type connections under longitudinal or lateral vibration
Applying the generalized transfer matrix formulation for elements with arbitrary input/output locations to vibration dynamic analysis of more complex engineering structures
independent_variables: Dynamic modeling and simulation approach (FEM with bonded contact, FCCFEM with frictional contact, T-TMM, C-TMM, E-TMM, FCCTMM, and experimental testing)
Bolted vibration system structural configuration (centrally symmetric ZS, mirror-symmetric NS-1, and mirror-symmetric NS-2)
Vibration mode evaluated (first bending mode versus second bending mode)
Excitation frequency range (0-1 kHz for ZS, 0-10 kHz for NS-1, 0-5 kHz for NS-2) and PZT driving signal phase difference (0 deg versus 180 deg)
Input and output point locations on single-input single-output (SISO) elastic elements (Type A, Type B, Type C)
limitations_inferred: The method was only experimentally verified on relatively simple planar beam-like assemblies and may require substantial extension for complex 3D continuum bodies or multi-bolt joint arrays
The formulation presumes static friction without continuous stick-slip transitions or dynamic slip evolution during large-amplitude cyclic oscillations
Long-term environmental factors such as operational temperature fluctuations, surface wear, and vibration-induced loosening are not incorporated into the dynamic model
Convergence of the iterative frictional contact correction relies on predefined convergence tolerances and could experience instability or sensitivity in more intricate multi-interface systems
limitations_stated_by_authors: The approach is primarily developed and validated for bending-dominated vibration modes where local interface lifting governs compliance behavior under pronounced component stiffness disparity
The model does not explicitly capture detailed contact mechanics or tangential micro-slip effects occurring in lap joints subjected to longitudinal or lateral vibrations

Predictive accuracy degrades notably for higher modes (such as the second bending mode) due to intrinsic TMM numerical ill-conditioning and overcorrection caused by simplified shear force distribution assumptions
Iterative evaluation of the correction coefficient introduces a modest computational time penalty compared to uncorrected or rigid-body TMM variants
main_results: FCCTMM achieved computational efficiency over 100 to 600 times faster than frictional contact finite element simulations (117x for ZS, 301x for NS-1, 601x for NS-2) while delivering comparable accuracy for the first mode

For the ZS assembly, FCCTMM predicted first and second mode frequencies of 63 Hz (3.07% error, MAC 0.99974) and 263 Hz (3.54% error, MAC 0.99272) in 6.34 s, markedly outperforming traditional TMM (10.77% and 11.81% error, MAC 0.88096 and 0.48599)
For the NS-1 assembly, FCCTMM achieved a first mode frequency of 3412 Hz (1.27% error, MAC 0.99926) in 20.94 s, compared to traditional TMM with 26.04% error (MAC 0.97164) and FCCFEM taking 6314.80 s

For the NS-2 assembly, FCCTMM predicted the first mode frequency with 1.28% error (551 Hz) and the second mode with -13.21% error (1701 Hz) in 21.41 s, compared to traditional TMM second-mode error of 34.33% and FCCFEM taking 12884.50 s

FCCTMM exhibited an overcorrection phenomenon in the second mode of NS-2, where the predicted frequency was substantially lower than experimental measurements due to disparate modal deformation between connecting plate and block

Experimental measurements identified an average first-slip friction coefficient of 0.20426 (CV 3.86%) and a linear torque-preload calibration of P = 433.54T + 129.32 (R^2 = 0.9173, yielding ~823 N preload at 1.6 N*m)
modeling_methods: Frictional Contact Correction Transfer Matrix Method (FCCTMM) with iterative angular correction
Traditional Transfer Matrix Method (T-TMM) assuming rigid connections and rigid SISO elements
Corrected Transfer Matrix Method (C-TMM) with frictional correction but rigid SISO elements
Elastic Transfer Matrix Method (E-TMM) with elastic SISO elements but rigid contact interfaces
Finite Element Method (FEM) under fully bonded contact interface assumptions in ANSYS 19.2
Frictional Contact Correction Finite Element Method (FCCFEM) using augmented Lagrangian contact formulation and Newton-Raphson solver in ANSYS 19.2
Timoshenko beam theory for longitudinal-bending coupled transfer matrices of elastic and piezoelectric beam elements
Planar motion transfer matrices of massless rigid bodies for arbitrary SISO coordinate transformations
Complex Young's modulus and loss factor formulation for material and piezoelectric damping
performance_metrics: Resonant frequency relative error percentage relative to experimental measurements
Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) values evaluating mode shape correlation
Computation time in seconds and speedup factor relative to finite element contact simulations
Iteration counts and convergence tolerances for the iterative contact correction process
Coefficient of variation (CV) for experimental friction coefficient and preload measurements
Coefficient of determination (R^2) for linear regression of the torque-preload relationship
possible_gap_implications: While formulated for bolted structural clamps, extending iterative contact-correction transfer matrix frameworks to flexible continuum joints and multi-layer interfaces could enable rapid, low-order dynamic modeling for variable-compliance robotic links without heavy nonlinear finite element meshes

The observed modal overcorrection and omission of tangential micro-slip underline the necessity of developing multi-modal, friction-coupled interface formulations to accurately model high-frequency dynamics in soft and flexible manipulators
paper.research_objective: To propose and experimentally validate a novel frictional contact correction transfer matrix method (FCCTMM) that accurately and efficiently models the vibration dynamics of bolted connection systems by iteratively accounting for interface compliance and deriving generalized elastic beam transfer matrices for arbitrary input/output locations.
paper.research_problem: Imperfect bolted interfaces in structural clamps and flanges exhibit semi-bonded and semi-free non-rigid contact characteristics that hinder accurate dynamic modeling and degrade computational efficiency, while traditional transfer matrix methods neglect bolted interface non-rigidity and input/output location shifts.
paper.title: A novel frictional contact correction transfer matrix method for bolted vibration systems: modeling, simulation, and experimental validation
